title: How Jon Ossoff Won
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: A year ago, he was the Senate's most vulnerable Democrat. On Tuesday, he won Georgia by 18 points. Here is how he did it.
cover_alt: Collage of Jon Ossoff and Mike Collins in front of a map of Georgia
cover_caption: Collage by Youth Outsider. Photos: Office of Sen. Jon Ossoff (public domain); U.S. House of Representatives (public domain). Map: U.S. Census Bureau boundaries.

figures.alt: Jon Ossoff at a 2020 campaign event

body:
In November 2025, Roll Call ranked Jon Ossoff the [most vulnerable senator](https://rollcall.com/2025/11/06/most-vulnerable-senators-2026-elections/) up for re-election in 2026. He was the only Democrat on the list from a state Donald Trump had carried, and Republicans had made his seat their top target.

On Tuesday, the race was called not long after polls closed. Ossoff beat Republican Rep. Mike Collins [59% to 41%](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/senate-results), an 18-point margin in a state Trump won by about two points in 2024. More than 3 million Georgians voted, a [record turnout](https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/11/04/senate-balance-line-county-by-county-map-georgias-ossoff-vs-collins-race/) for a midterm.

A national wave helped. But Ossoff's margin was among the largest of any Democrat in a competitive state, and it came from decisions he and his campaign made long before the wave arrived.

## He got the opponent Republicans didn't want

Republican leaders in Washington spent much of 2025 trying to recruit Gov. Brian Kemp, who won re-election in 2022 by nearly eight points and was seen as the party's strongest possible candidate. Kemp said no. He then backed Derek Dooley, a former college football coach who had never run for office.

Trump went another way. Collins, a trucking-company owner who represents Georgia's 10th District, led a crowded May primary with [40.5%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_Senate_election_in_Georgia), won Trump's endorsement and beat Dooley in a June runoff, 55.5% to 44.5%. The fight left Georgia Republicans split between their governor and their president, and left them with a nominee who had never run statewide.

Collins then spent much of the fall on defense. He faced a House Ethics inquiry over his office's hiring of his former chief of staff's girlfriend, which he called meritless, and reports that his son-in-law had shared antisemitic and white nationalist posts. Collins said he did not share those views. His campaign also drew criticism for an [AI-generated video](https://www.newsweek.com/democrats-score-early-win-with-jon-ossoff-over-mike-collins-in-georgia-12659579) that put invented words in Ossoff's mouth.

## He raised more money than anyone

Ossoff was the Senate's top fundraiser of the cycle, with [$136.6 million](https://rollcall.com/2026/11/03/senate-democrats-results-midterm-elections/) through mid-October. Collins had raised $10.7 million. Late in the race, Ossoff had [about $26 million](https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/10/jon-ossoff-widens-fundraising-edge-over-mike-collins/) in the bank to Collins's roughly $1 million.

The money let Ossoff stay on television across the state for months and pay for a statewide campaign Collins couldn't match. He also used it to help the rest of the ticket, moving more than $3.6 million into the Georgia Democratic Party's coordinated campaign, which also supported Keisha Lance Bottoms in the governor's race. As the race slipped away from Collins, Republican outside groups [pulled back](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/ossoff-wins-democrats-hold-firm-georgia-republicans-fail-flip-prized-senate-seat) in the final weeks.

## He talked about costs

Collins ran on immigration and inflation. He wrote the Laken Riley Act, the immigrant detention law named for a Georgia nursing student killed in 2024, and argued that Ossoff's votes had driven up prices and taxes.

Ossoff answered with costs of his own. He tied Collins to Trump's tariffs, to Republican-backed Medicaid cuts and to the war with Iran, which had pushed gas past [$4.50 a gallon](https://abc7ny.com/post/average-us-gas-prices-top-450-gallon-highest-4-years/19050172/) in the spring. Those were the issues voters said they cared about most. In NBC's national exit poll, 39% named the economy as their top issue, and 87% said they were concerned about the cost of gas and diesel.

## He was the most magnetic candidate in the race

Most senators are known in their home states. Ossoff became something closer to a celebrity.

Part of it is how he talks. He speaks slowly and evenly, even when he is landing his sharpest lines, and for six years he has built a reputation for committee-room exchanges in which he questions Trump's appointees calmly, lets them get flustered and then posts the clip. His campaign was built to travel online. Its rallies were livestreamed from multiple cameras, often shot from below in a signature frame critics and fans alike called [the "Ossoff angle,"](https://www.dailywire.com/news/democrat-presidential-hopeful-is-ripping-off-the-obama-playbook-right-down-to-the-camera-angle) and compared to Barack Obama's 2008 imagery.

Part of it is how he looks. Fan-made edits of his rallies and Senate hearings, cut like videos of a pop star or a TV president, [spread for months](https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/jon-ossoff-georgia-re-election-tiktok-edits-1830047) on TikTok and Instagram, especially among young voters who don't usually follow politics. The Democratic Party's own TikTok account gave him what Axios called the ["thirst trap" treatment](https://axios.com/2026/08/18/democrats-social-media-ossoff-el-sayed), and fans nicknamed him "Senator My Boo." Democratic strategists told The 19th the attention was free publicity that could turn scrolling into donations, volunteers and votes. Republicans noticed too. A GOP-aligned super PAC ran AI-generated ads mocking his spending on hair and makeup, which Ossoff condemned.

And part of it is that he was willing to provoke. In August, at a rally in Atlanta, he went after Trump directly, saying the president [*"sleeps through his meetings, he golfs, and trades stocks,"*](https://keyt.com/politics/cnn-us-politics/2026/08/17/ossoff-targets-a-close-trump-aide-launching-a-personal-feud-with-the-white-house-as-midterms-loom/) and that he wants to *"travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace,"* a reference to Trump's executive assistant, Natalie Harp, and the jet Qatar gave the administration. Some on his own side, including Obama strategist David Axelrod, called the line about Harp unnecessary. But the White House [took the bait](https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/08/18/flying-palace-vs-pee-wee-herman-ossoff-trump-feud-explodes-georgia-senate-race/). Trump called Ossoff a "Pee-wee Herman look-alike," and a White House spokesman called him a "cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama." For a week, the president of the United States was arguing with a senator from Georgia. It gave Ossoff attention money can't buy and made the race about Trump at a moment when Trump's approval was falling.

## The wave did the rest

By Election Day, that approval had fallen to [38%](https://www.dailysignal.com/2026/11/04/iran-war-plays-major-role-in-midterm-blowout/) in exit polling. Gas prices, the Iran war and Trump's own conduct pushed voters toward Democrats across the country, and Georgia was no exception. Democrats also won the governor's office there for the first time since 1998.

Still, many Democrats rode the same wave and won by a few points. Ossoff won by 18, in a state that was supposed to be a tossup. Six years of quiet constituent work, which even some Republican officials [respected](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/news-from-npr/2026-11-03/jon-ossoff-wins-reelection-in-georgia-easily-defeating-republican-mike-collins), gave him a cushion many of them didn't have.

## What comes next

The question now is whether he stays in the Senate. At an October debate, Ossoff was asked whether he would serve a full six-year term. [*"Yes, I will,"*](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/dem-senator-says-zero-interest-running-president-debate-gop-opponent) he said. *"I have zero interest in running for president."*

In 2006, a young senator named Barack Obama gave a similar answer. Two years later, he was elected president. Ossoff is 39, has more money than anyone in his party and has just won a Trump state by 18 points. He will be asked again.
